title: Constructors
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of constructors in a C#/.NET program.
Predict the result of the included C# example and verify the documented output.
Apply constructors to a small task and identify one relevant boundary, limitation, or version requirement.

content.intro: Constructors is lesson 75 in Object-Oriented Programming Fundamentals. Object-oriented design groups state and behavior behind a useful contract. Keep internal state valid and expose only the operations that callers need.
content.why_it_matters: Encapsulation keeps objects valid and limits the amount of state other code must understand. This lesson focuses on constructors and shows how to verify the behavior instead of relying on assumptions.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Object-oriented design groups state and behavior behind a useful contract. Keep internal state valid and expose only the operations that callers need.

content_blocks.title: A practical way to learn it
content_blocks.text: Start with the smallest valid case for constructors. Predict the output, run or inspect the example in the stated toolchain, then change one input or rule and compare the result. For production code, record assumptions and verify boundary cases.

items.title: Constructor chaining
items.text: Keep object invariants valid at construction and mutation boundaries. Constructors establish required state, while properties can control changes; init and required improve initialization intent but do not replace validation.

content.task: Try it yourself: create a small C# example that demonstrates constructors. Change one input or implementation detail, predict the result, then check it locally and explain one edge case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates constructors rather than only repeating its definition.
The result is checked locally or against a clearly documented reference output.
At least one relevant boundary, invalid-input case, or compatibility condition is considered.
hints: List the assumptions and expected behavior for constructors before editing the code.
Change one variable or rule at a time; keep the previous output for comparison.
If behavior differs, confirm the compiler/target framework and consult the linked official documentation.
content.solution_notes: Suggested approach: identify the expected input and output, start from the smallest example, use the feature only where it clarifies the rule, and verify both a typical case and a boundary/failure case.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming the feature works identically on every target
common_mistakes.why: Language syntax, libraries, and runtime support are version-dependent.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the target framework and official versioned reference before using the feature.

common_mistakes.why: Boundary values, malformed input, and failure states often expose the real bug.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one typical input and one boundary or invalid case to the manual or automated checks.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating sample output as proof that the code ran
common_mistakes.why: The course reader uses static reference output for C# because it has no C# execution runner.
common_mistakes.fix: Run the snippet in a local .NET project or a separately isolated execution service.
